entries.9f1ad31991fcc5262503eca32703e1df4c2cb8c9: <div sID="gen13003" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="128" osisID="Ps.128" sID="Ps.128"/> <div eID="gen13003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13004" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13005" type="x-p"/> This, as the former, is a psalm for families. In that we were taught that the prosperity of our families depends upon the blessing of God; in this we are taught that the only way to obtain that blessing which will make our families comfortable is to live in the fear of God and in obedience to him. Those that do so, in general, shall be blessed (<reference osisRef="Ps.128.1-Ps.128.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.128.4">4</reference>), In particular, I. They shall be prosperous and successful in their employments, <reference osisRef="Ps.128.2">ver. 2</reference>. II. Their relations shall be agreeable, <reference osisRef="Ps.128.3">ver. 3</reference>. III. They shall live to see their families brought up, <reference osisRef="Ps.128.6">ver. 6</reference>. IV. They shall have the satisfaction of seeing the church of God in a flourishing condition, <reference osisRef="Ps.128.5-Ps.128.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. We must sing this psalm in the firm belief of this truth, That religion and piety are the best friends to outward prosperity, giving God the praise that it is so and that we have found it so, and encouraging ourselves and others with it.
entries.6913b5ba7f5ffae71564e99cda9efe9504a36b1d: <div eID="gen13005" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13004" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Blessedness of the Godly.</title> <div sID="gen13006" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> every one that feareth the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; that walketh in his ways. 2 For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy <hi type="italic">shalt</hi> thou <hi type="italic">be,</hi> and <hi type="italic">it shall be</hi> well with thee. 3 Thy wife <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> as a fruitful vine by the sides of thine house: thy children like olive plants round about thy table. <hi type="super">4</hi> Behold, that thus shall the man be blessed that feareth the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">5</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall bless thee out of Zion: and thou shalt see the good of Jerusalem all the days of thy life. 6 Yea, thou shalt see thy children's children, <hi type="italic">and</hi> peace upon Israel. <div eID="gen13006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13007" type="x-p"/> It is here shown that godliness has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come. <div eID="gen13007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13008" type="x-p"/> I. It is here again and again laid down as an undoubted truth that <hi type="italic">those who are truly holy are truly happy.</hi> Those whose blessed state we are here assured of are such as <hi type="italic">fear the Lord</hi> and <hi type="italic">walk in his ways,</hi> such as have a deep reverence of God upon their spirits and evidence it by a regular and constant conformity to his will. Where the fear of God is a commanding principle in the heart the tenour of the conversation will be accordingly; and in vain do we pretend to be of those that fear God if we do not make conscience both of keeping to his ways and not trifling in them or drawing back. Such are blessed (<reference osisRef="Ps.128.1">v. 1</reference>), and shall be blessed, <reference osisRef="Ps.128.4">v. 4</reference>. God blesses them, and his pronouncing them blessed makes them so. They are blessed now, they shall be blessed still, and for ever. This blessedness, arising from this blessing, is here secured, 1. To all the saints universally: <hi type="italic">Blessed is everyone that fears the Lord,</hi> whoever he be; in every nation he that fears God and works righteousness is accepted of him, and therefore is blessed whether he be high or low, rich or poor, in the world; if religion rule him, it will protect and enrich him. 2. To such a saint in particular: <hi type="italic">Thus shall the man be blessed,</hi> not only the nation, the church in its public capacity, but the particular person in his private interests. 3. We are encouraged to apply it to ourselves (<reference osisRef="Ps.128.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Happy shalt thou be;</hi> thou mayest take the comfort of the promise, and expect the benefit of it, as if it were directed to thee by name, if thou <hi type="italic">fear God and walk in his ways. Happy shalt thou be,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">It shall be well with thee;</hi> whatever befals thee, good shall be brought out of it; it shall be well with thee while thou livest, better when thou diest, and best of all to eternity." It is asserted (<reference osisRef="Ps.128.4">v. 4</reference>) with a note commanding attention: <hi type="italic">Behold, thus shall the man be blessed;</hi> behold it by faith in the promise; behold it by observation in the performance of the promise; behold it with assurance that it shall be so, for God is faithful, and with admiration that it should be so, for we merit no favour, no blessing, from him. <div eID="gen13008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13009" type="x-p"/> II. Particular promises are here made to godly people, which they may depend upon, as far as is for God's glory and their good; and that is enough. <div eID="gen13009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13010" type="x-p"/> 1. That, by the blessing of God, they shall get an honest livelihood and live comfortably upon it. It is not promised that they shall live at ease, without care or pains, but, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt eat the labour of thy hands.</hi> Here is a double promise, (1.) That they shall have something to do (for an idle life is a miserable uncomfortable life) and shall have health, and strength, and capacity of mind to do it, and shall not be forced to be beholden to others for necessary food, and to live, as the disabled poor do, upon the labours of other people. It is as much a mercy as it is a duty <hi type="italic">with quietness</hi> to <hi type="italic">work and eat our own bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.12">2 Thess. 3.12</reference>. (2.) That they shall succeed in their employments, and they and theirs shall enjoy what they get; others shall not come and eat the bread out of their mouths, nor shall it be taken from them either by oppressive rulers or invading enemies. God will not blast it and blow upon it (as he did, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.9">Hag. 1.9</reference>), and his blessing will make a little go a great way. It is very pleasant to enjoy the fruits of our own industry; as the sleep, so the food, of a labouring man is sweet. <div eID="gen13010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13011" type="x-p"/> 2. That they shall have abundance of comfort in their family-relations. As a wife and children are very much a man's care, so, if by the grace of God they are such as they should be, they are very much a man's delight, as much as any creature-comfort. (1.) The <hi type="italic">wife</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">as a vine by the sides of the house,</hi> not only as a spreading vine which serves for an ornament, but as a fruitful vine which is for profit, and with the fruit whereof both God and man are honoured, <reference osisRef="Judg.9.13">Judg. ix. 13</reference>. The vine is a weak and tender plant, and needs to be supported and cherished, but it is a very valuable plant, and some think (because all the products of it were prohibited to the Nazarites) it was the <hi type="italic">tree of knowledge</hi> itself. The wife's place is the husband's house; there her business lies, and that is her castle. <hi type="italic">Where is Sarah thy wife? Behold, in the tent;</hi> where should she be else? Her place is <hi type="italic">by the sides of the house,</hi> not under-foot to be trampled on, nor yet upon the house-top to domineer (if she be so, she is but <hi type="italic">as the grass upon the house-top,</hi> in the next psalm), but on the side of the house, being a rib out of the side of the man. She shall be a loving wife, as the vine, which cleaves to the house-side, an obedient wife, as the vine, which is pliable, and grows as it is directed. She shall be fruitful as the vine, not only in children, but in the fruits of wisdom, and righteousness, and good management, the <hi type="italic">branches</hi> of which <hi type="italic">run over the wall</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.22">Gen. xlix. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.11">Ps. lxxx. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">like a fruitful vine,</hi> not cumbering the ground, nor bringing forth sour grapes, or grapes of Sodom, but good fruit. (2.) The <hi type="italic">children</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">as olive plants,</hi> likely in time to be olive-trees, and, though <hi type="italic">wild by nature,</hi> yet grafted into the good olive, and partaking of its <hi type="italic">root and fatness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.17">Rom. xi. 17</reference>. It is pleasant to parents who have a table spread, though but with ordinary fare, to see their children round about it, to have many children, enough to surround it, and those with them, and not scattered, or the parents forced from them. Job makes it one of the first instances of his former prosperity that <hi type="italic">his children were about him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.29.5">Job xxix. 5</reference>. Parents love to have their children at table, to keep up the pleasantness of the table-talk, to have them in health, craving food and not physic, to have them like <hi type="italic">olive-plants,</hi> straight and green, sucking in the sap of their good education, and likely in due time to be serviceable. <div eID="gen13011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13012" type="x-p"/> 3. That they shall have those things which God has promised and which they pray for: <hi type="italic">The Lord shall bless thee out of Zion,</hi> where the ark of the covenant was, and where the pious Israelites attended with their devotions. <hi type="italic">Blessings out of Zion</hi> are the best-blessings, which flow, not from common providence, but from special grace, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.2">Ps. xx. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen13012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13013" type="x-p"/> 4. That they shall live long, to enjoy the comforts of the rising generations: "Thou shalt <hi type="italic">see thy children's children,</hi> as Joseph, <reference osisRef="Gen.50.23">Gen. l. 23</reference>. Thy family shall be built up and continued, and thou shalt have the pleasure of seeing it." <hi type="italic">Children's children,</hi> if they be good children, <hi type="italic">are the crown of old men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.17.6">Prov. xvii. 6</reference>), who are apt to be fond of their grandchildren. <div eID="gen13013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13014" type="x-p"/> 5. That they shall see the welfare of God's church, and the land of their nativity, which every man who fears God is no less concerned for than for the prosperity of his own family. "Thou shalt be blessed in Zion's blessing, and wilt think thyself so. Thou shalt <hi type="italic">see the good of Jerusalem</hi> as long as thou shalt live, though thou shouldest live long, and shalt not have thy private comforts allayed and embittered by public troubles." A good man can have little comfort in seeing his children's children, unless withal he see peace upon Israel, and have hopes of transmitting the entail of religion pure and entire to those that shall come after him, for that is the best inheritance.  <chapter eID="Ps.128"/> <div eID="gen13014" type="x-p"/>

entries.ce0c333d7b7abd16d5f75180ff1140292f8e7089: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7022"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 128</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.128.1-Ps.128.6">Psa 128:1-6</reference>. The temporal blessings of true piety. The eighth chapter of Zecariah is a virtual commentary on this Psalm. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.128.3">Psa 128:3</reference> with <reference osisRef="Zech.8.5">Zec 8:5</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Ps.128.2">Psa 128:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="Lev.26.16">Le 26:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.33">De 28:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.8.10">Zec 8:10</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Ps.128.6">Psa 128:6</reference></title> <div sID="gen10775" type="x-p"/> with <reference osisRef="Zech.8.4">Zec 8:4</reference>.<div eID="gen10775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10776" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7022"/>1. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>). <div eID="gen10776" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f02506934d067c9dfce356acee099518accb47b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7023"/><div sID="gen10777" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7023"/><hi type="bold">2. For thou shalt eat--</hi>that is, It is a blessing to live on the fruits of one's own industry. <div eID="gen10777" type="x-p"/>
entries.674853084b7855ecb95dac0f035d36aeb0024856: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7024"/><div sID="gen10778" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7024"/><hi type="bold">3. by the sides--</hi>or, "within" (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Psa 48:2</reference>).<div eID="gen10778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10779" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">olive plants--</hi>are peculiarly luxuriant (<reference osisRef="Ps.52.8">Psa 52:8</reference>). <div eID="gen10779" type="x-p"/>
entries.48653d5c6a3c3a412ab7196987686c6047f3199c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7025"/><div sID="gen10780" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7025"/>5. In temporal blessings the pious do not forget the richer blessings of God's grace, which they shall ever enjoy. <div eID="gen10780" type="x-p"/>
entries.506e6eab27cf53c2c3341cd9ada9977601e54ede: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7026"/><div sID="gen10781" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7026"/>6. Long life crowns all other temporal favors. As <reference osisRef="Ps.125.5">Psa 125:5</reference>, this Psalm closes with a prayer for peace, with prosperity for God's people. <chapter eID="Ps.128"/>

entries.9144bfd337b24fa666fa6c68d24e0e8b3342eb1e: <div eID="gen23120" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23121" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23122" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23122" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23121" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23123" type="x-p"/> The blessedness of the man that fears the Lord, <reference osisRef="Psa.128.1">Psa 128:1</reference>. He is blessed in his labor, <reference osisRef="Psa.128.2">Psa 128:2</reference>; in his wife and children, <reference osisRef="Psa.128.3">Psa 128:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.128.4">Psa 128:4</reference>; in the ordinances of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.128.5">Psa 128:5</reference>; and in a long life and numerous posterity, <reference osisRef="Psa.128.6">Psa 128:6</reference>. <div eID="gen23123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23124" type="x-p"/> This Psalm has no title, either in the Hebrew or any of the Versions; though the Syriac supposes it to have been spoken of Zerubbabel, prince of Judah, who was earnestly engaged in building the temple of the Lord. It seems to be a continuation of the preceding Psalm, or rather the second part of it. The man who is stated to have a numerous offspring, in the preceding Psalm, is here represented as sitting at table with his large family. A person in the mean while coming in, sees his happy state, speaks of his comforts, and predicts to him and his all possible future good. And why? Because the man and his family "fear God, and walk in his ways."
entries.f1baa68950dea4d1da8afec30e4254b6acd3f0a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23125" type="x-p"/> Those shalt eat the labor of thine hands - Thou shalt not be exempted from labor. Thou shalt work: But God will bless and prosper that work, and thou and thy family shall eat of it. Ye shall all live on the produce of your own labor, and the hand of violence shall not be permitted to deprive you of it. Thus, <div eID="gen23125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23126" type="x-p"/> Happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee - Thou shalt have prosperity.
entries.5c0e14ef8fef98df6de14940eefbed38865f5c0c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23127" type="x-p"/> Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine - Thy children, in every corner and apartment of thy house, shall be the evidences of the fruitfulness of thy wife, as bunches of grapes on every bough of the vine are the proofs of its being in a healthy thriving state. Being about the house sides, or apartments, is spoken of the wife, not the vine; being around the table is spoken of the children, not of the olive-plants. It does not appear that there were any vines planted against the walls of the houses in Jerusalem, nor any olive-trees in pots or tubs in the inside of their houses; as may be found in different parts of Europe.
entries.eb4868ca0c8abf93eff5f868a4a186d6108b2a75: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23128" type="x-p"/> Thus shall the man be blessed that feareth the Lord - A great price for a small consideration. Fear God, and thou shalt have as much domestic good as may be useful to thee.
entries.873b454b552dd9c451c2361d437b539da7b9d998: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23129" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall bless thee out of Zion - In all thy approaches to him in his house by prayer, by sacrifice, and by offering, thou shalt have his especial blessing. Thou shalt thrive every where, and in all things. <div eID="gen23129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23130" type="x-p"/> And thou shalt see the good of Jerusalem - Thou shalt see the cause of God flourish in thy lifetime, and his Church in great prosperity.
entries.ae427ef11aebdb2d93fd7b77918a9ab813b9e972: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23131" type="x-p"/> Yea, thou shalt see thy children's children - Thou shall not die till thou have seen thy family all settled in the world, and those of them who may be married blessed with children. <div eID="gen23131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23132" type="x-p"/> And peace upon Israel - This is the same conclusion as in <reference osisRef="Psa.125.1-Psa.125.5">Psa 125:1-5</reference>; and should be translated, Peace be upon Israel! May God favor his own cause, and bless all his people!  <chapter eID="Ps.128"/> <div eID="gen23132" type="x-p"/>

entries.ef0408a13e293d90730ee9052bff4d522d8556ec: <div eID="gen10202" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Family Prosperity of the God-Fearing Man</title> <div sID="gen10203" type="x-p"/> Just as <reference osisRef="Ps.127.1-Ps.127.5">Psa 127:1-5</reference> is appended to <reference osisRef="Ps.126.1-Ps.126.6">Psa 126:1-6</reference> because the fact that Israel was so surprised by the redemption out of exile that they thought they were dreaming, finds its interpretation in the universal truth that God bestows upon him whom He loves, in sleep, that which others are not able to acquire by toiling and moiling the day and night: so <reference osisRef="Ps.128.1-Ps.128.6">Psa 128:1-6</reference> follows <reference osisRef="Ps.127.1-Ps.127.5">Psa 127:1-5</reference> for the same reason as <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1-Ps.2.12">Psa 2:1-12</reference> follows <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>-6. In both instances they are Psalms placed together, of which one begins with <hi type="italic">ashrê</hi> and one ends with <hi type="italic">ashrê .</hi> In other respects <reference osisRef="Ps.128.1-Ps.128.6">Psa 128:1-6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.127.1-Ps.127.5">Psa 127:1-5</reference> supplement one another. They are related to one another much as the New Testament parables of the treasure in the field and the one pearl are related. That which makes man happy is represented in <reference osisRef="Ps.127.1-Ps.127.5">Psa 127:1-5</reference> as a gift coming as a blessing, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.128.1-Ps.128.6">Psa 128:1-6</reference> as a reward coming as a blessing, that which is briefly indicated in the word שׂכר in <reference osisRef="Ps.127.3">Psa 127:3</reference> being here expanded and unfolded. There it appears as a gift of grace in contrast to the God-estranged self-activity of man, here as a fruit of the <hi type="italic">ora et labora</hi>. Ewald considers this and the preceding Psalm to be songs to be sung at table. But they are ill-suited for this purpose; for they contain personal mirrorings instead of petitions, and instead of benedictions of those who are about to partake of the food provided.
entries.5b7b20a7313cbef680524d94ab22bfd1be5835d6: <reference osisRef="Ps.128.1-Ps.128.3">Psa 128:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen10203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10204" type="x-p"/> The כּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.128.2">Psa 128:2</reference> signifies neither “for” (Aquila, κόπον τῶν ταρσῶν σου ὅτι φάγεσαι), nor “when” (Symmachus, κόπον χειρῶν σου ἐωθίων); it is the directly affirmative כּי, which is sometimes thus placed after other words in a clause (<reference osisRef="Ps.118.10-Ps.118.12">Psa 118:10-12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.20">Gen 18:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.41.32">Gen 41:32</reference>). The proof in favour of this asseverating כּי is the very usual כּי עתּה in the apodoses of hypothetical protases, or even כּי־אז in <reference osisRef="Job.11.15">Job 11:15</reference>, or also only כּי in <reference osisRef="Isa.7.9">Isa 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.39">1Sa 14:39</reference>; “surely then;” the transition from the confirmative to the affirmative signification is evident from <reference osisRef="Ps.128.4">Psa 128:4</reference> of the Psalm before us. To support one’s self by one’s own labour is a duty which even a Paul did not wish to avoid (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.34">Act 20:34</reference>), and so it is a great good fortune (טוב לך as in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.71">Psa 119:71</reference>) to eat the produce of the labour of one’s own hands (lxx , τοὺς καρποὺς τῶν πόνων, or according to an original reading, τοὺς πὸνους τῶν καρπῶν);<note placement="foot">The fact that the τῶν καρπῶν of the lxx here, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.31.20">Pro 31:20</reference>, is intended to refer to the hands is noted by Theodoret and also by Didymus (in Rosenmuller): καρποὺς φησὶνῦν ὡς ἀπὸ μέρους τὰς χεῖρας (i.e., <hi type="italic">per synecdochen partis pro toto</hi>), τουτέστι τῶν πρακτικῶν σου δυνάμεων φάγεσαι τοὺς πόνους.</note> <div eID="gen10204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10205" type="x-p"/> For he who can make himself useful to others and still is also independent of them, he eats the bread of blessing which God gives, which is sweeter than the bread of charity which men give. In close connection with this is the prosperity of a house that is at peace and contented within itself, of an amiable and tranquil and hopeful (rich in hope) family life. “Thy wife (אשׁתּך, found only here, for אשׁתּך) is as a fruit-producing vine.” פּריּה for פּרה, from פּרה = פּרי, with the <hi type="italic">Jod</hi> of the root retained, like בוכיּה, Lam 1:16. The figure of the vine is admirably suited to the wife, who is a shoot or sprig of the husband, and stands in need of the man’s support as the vine needs a stick or the wall of a house (<hi type="italic">pergula</hi>). בּירכּתי ביתך does not belong to the figure, as Kimchi is of opinion, who thinks of a vine starting out of the room and climbing up in the open air outside. What is meant is the angle, corner, or nook (ירכּתי, in relation to things and artificial, equivalent to the natural ירכי), i.e., the background, the privacy of the house, where the housewife, who is not to be seen much out of doors, leads a quiet life, entirely devoted to the happiness of her husband and her family. The children springing from such a nobel vine, planted around the family table, are like olive shoots or cuttings; cf. in Euripides, <hi type="italic">Medea</hi>, 1098: τέκνων ἐν οἴκοις γλυκερὸν βλάστημα, and <hi type="italic">Herc</hi>. <hi type="italic">Fur</hi>. 839: καλλίπαις στέφανος. thus fresh as young layered small olive-trees and thus promising are they.
entries.15597bae892072e376755a46f0db19686d22bf2a: <reference osisRef="Ps.128.4-Ps.128.6">Psa 128:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen10205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10206" type="x-p"/> Pointing back to this charming picture of family life, the poet goes on to say: behold, for thus = behold, thus is the man actually blessed who fears Jahve. כּי confirms the reality of the matter of fact to which the הנּה points. The promissory future in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.128.5">Psa 128:5</reference></hi> is followed by imperatives which call upon the God-fearing man at once to do that which, in accordance with the promises, stands before him as certain. מציּון as in <reference osisRef="Ps.134.3">Psa 134:3</reference>; Psa 20:3. בּנים לבניך instead of בּני בניך gives a designed indefiniteness to the first member of the combination. Every blessing the individual enjoys comes from the God of salvation, who has taken up His abode in Zion, and is perfected in participation in the prosperity of the holy city and of the whole church, of which it is the centre. A New Testament song would here open up the prospect of the heavenly Jerusalem. But the character of limitation to this present world that is stamped upon the Old Testament does not admit of this. The promise refers only to a present participation in the well-being of Jerusalem (Zec 8:15) and to long life prolonged in one’s children’s children; and in this sense calls down intercessorily peace upon Israel in all its members, and in all places and all ages.  <chapter eID="Ps.128"/> <div eID="gen10206" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 128
This Psalm is akin to the preceding, and, so to speak, a kind of appendage to it; for it declares that the divine blessing, to the diffusion of which among the whole human race Solomon testified, is to be seen most conspicuously in the ease of God’s true and sincere servants.
A Song of Degrees.
Psalm 128:1-3
1. Blessed is the man who feareth Jehovah, and walketh in his ways. 2. For when thou shalt eat the labor of thy hands, thou shalt be blessed, and it shall be well with thee. 3. Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine on the sides of thy house, and thy children as olive plants around thy table.
“The tables of the Jews, as we may hence (and from 1 Samuel 16:11) infer, were round: they had sobs (Ezekiel 23:41) placed about them, on which (Genesis 27:19; Judges 10:6; 1 Samuel 2:5, 24, 25; 1 Kings 13:20) they sat, excepting at the Paschal feast.” — Cresswell. In the Illustrated Commentary upon the Bible, the writer on this passage objects to the common reading — Fruitful vine by the sides of thine house. olive-plants round about thy table. “We do not remember,” says he, “to have met with a single instance in the East of vines trained against the walls of a house, or of olives near or about a house. Neither have we read of such instances. The passage doubtless derives its figures from the fertility of the vine, and from the appearance of the olive, or the order in which olive-trees are planted.” He accordingly proposes the following construction — “Thy wife, on the sides (interior apartments) of thy house, shall be as the fruitful vine; and thy children, round about thy table, like olive-plants.”
 
1 Blessed is the man who feareth Jehovah. In the preceding Psalm it was stated that prosperity in all human affairs, and in the whole course of our life, is to be hoped for exclusively from the grace of God; and now the Prophet admonishes us that those who desire to be partakers of the blessing of God must with sincerity of heart devote themselves wholly to him; for he will never disappoint those who serve him. The first verse contains a summary of the subject-matter of the Psalm; the remaining portion being added only by way of exposition. The maxim “that those are blessed who fear God, especially in the present life,” is so much with variance with the common opinion of men, that very few will give it their assent. Everywhere are to be found fluttering about many Epicureans, similar to Dionysius, who, having once had a favorable wind upon the sea and a prosperous voyage, after having plundered a temple,
“Lequel true fois ayant bon vent sur mer, et la navigation prospore apres avoir pille une temple.” — Fr.
boasted that the gods favored church robbers. Also the weak are troubled and shaken by the prosperity of evil men, and they next faint under the load of their own miseries. The despisers of God may not indeed enjoy prosperity, and the condition of good men may be tolerable, but still the greater part of men are blind in considering the providence of God, or seem not in any degree to perceive it. The adage, “That it is best not to be born at all, or to die as soon as possible,” has certainly been long since received by the common consent of almost all men. Finally, carnal reason judges either that all mankind without exception are miserable, or that fortune is more favorable to ungodly and wicked men than to the good. To the sentiment that those are blessed who fear the Lord, it has an entire aversion, as I have declared at length on Psalm 37. So much the more requisite then is it to dwell upon the consideration of this truth. Farther, as this blessedness is not apparent to the eye, it is of importance, in order to our being able to apprehend it., first to attend to the definition which will ]be given of it by and bye, and secondly, to know that it depends chiefly upon the protection of God. Although we collect together all the circumstances which seem to contribute to a happy life, surely nothing will be found more desirable than to be kept hidden under the guardianship of God. If this blessing is, in our estimation, to be preferred, as it deserves, to all other good things, whoever is persuaded that the care of God is exercised about the world and human affairs, will at the same time unquestionably acknowledge that what is here laid down is the chief point of happiness.
But before I proceed farther, it is to be noticed that in the second part of the verse there is with good reason added a mark by which the servants of God are distinguished from those who despise him. We see how the most depraved, with no less pride than audacity and mockery, boast of fearing God. The Prophet therefore requires the attestation of the life as to this; for these two things, the fear of God and the keeping of his law, are inseparable; and the root must necessarily produce its corresponding fruit. Farther, we learn from this passage that our life does not meet with the divine approbation, except it be framed according to the divine law. There is unquestionably no religion without the fear of God, and from this fear the Prophet represents our living according to the commandment and ordinance of God as proceeding.

                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXXVIII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:head>A song of degrees.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm contains a description of the blessedness of good men.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 BLessed <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> every one that feareth the LORD: that walketh in his ways.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isai. 3. 10.</ns0:note> For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Thy labour shall not be vain and fruitless, and the fruit of thy labours shall not be taken away from thee and possessed by others, as God threatned to the disobedient, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28. but enjoyed by thy self with comfort and satisfaction.</ns0:note>: happy <ns0:hi>shalt</ns0:hi> thou be, and <ns0:hi>it shall be</ns0:hi> well with thee <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Both in this world and in the world to come, as even the Chaldee Paraphrast explains these words.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Thy wife <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> as a fruitful vine <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Like the vine for fruitfulness: or, like that sort of vines known by this name for its eminent fruitfulness, as some trees amongst us are for the same reason called <ns0:hi>the great bearers.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> by the sides of thine house <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Where the vines are commonly planted for support and other advantages. Which being applied to the wife, may signifie either, 1. the wife's duty to abide at home, <ns0:hi>Tit.</ns0:hi> 2. 5. as the harlot is deciphered by her gadding abroad, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 7. 11, 12. or rather, 2. the legitimateness of the children, which are begotten at home by the husband, and not abroad by strangers.</ns0:note>: thy children like olive<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plants <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Numerous, growing and flourishing, good both for ornament and manifold uses, as Olive-trees are.</ns0:note> round about thy table <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Where they shall sit at meat with thee, for thy comfort and safety.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Behold, that thus shall the man be blessed, that feareth the LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 The LORD shall bless thee out of Zion <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">From the Ark in <ns0:hi>Zion,</ns0:hi> and with those spiritual and everlasting blessings which are to be had no where but in <ns0:hi>Zion</ns0:hi> and from the God who dwelleth in <ns0:hi>Zion,</ns0:hi> and with all other mercies which thou shalt ask of God in <ns0:hi>Zion.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>: and thou shalt see the good of Jerusalem <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The prosperity of that City to which thou belongest, and which is the onely seat of Gods special presence and of his Worship, whose felicity therefore is very delightful to every good man, and upon whose peace the peace and safety of every member of it depends, as every seaman is concerned in the safety of the ship, in which he is.</ns0:note>, all the days of thy life.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Yea, thou shalt see thy childrens children, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 125. 5.</ns0:note> peace upon Israel <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Not onely upon <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> and the parts adjacent, but upon all the Tribes and people of <ns0:hi>Israel.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
